A machine at a large factory fills bottles with juice. To reduce the likelihood of bottles containing less than 8 ounces (oz) of juice, the machine is set to fill the bottles with a mean of $8.050 %$ of juice. To investigate whether the machine is working properly, the factory manager randomly samples ten bottles every 24 hours and records data for several variables from each of the sampled bottles.

Which of the following is classified as a continuous quantitative variable for the factory manager's investigation?
(A) Whether a randomly chosen bottle contains less than 8 oz of juice
(B) Whether all of the bottles in the sample contain less than 8 oz of juice
(C) The number of bottles that contain less than 8 oz of juice out of a random sample of 10 bottles of juice
(D) The number of properly filled bottles of juice at a randomly selected time
(E) The amount of juice, in ounces, in a randomly selected bottle

The following boxplot summarizes the annual snowfall amounts, in inches, for a sample of 25 cities in the United States.

Based on the boxplot, which of the following can be concluded?
(A) The first quartile is about 20 inches.
(B) The median is about 20 inches.
(C) The third quartile is about 30 inches.
(D) The interquartile range is about 20 inches.
(E) The range is about 40 inches.

According to a survey, 32 percent of people in a certain country regularly recycle. Mr. Giovanni, the mayor of a specific city in the country, wanted to know whether the residents in his city regularly recycle more than the national average. He selected a random sample of 50 residents, 28 of whom regularly recycle. Mr. Giovanni would like to use a one-sample $z$-test for a population proportion to test the hypotheses $H_{0}: p=0.32$ versus $H_{a}: p>0.32$, where $p$ is the proportion of city residents who regularly recycle. In order to use this test, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion needs to be approximately normal.

Which of the following is true for Mr. Giovanni's study and ensures that the sampling distribution of the sample proportion is approximately normal?
(A) The distribution of the population of all residents who regularly recycle is approximately normal.
(B) The sample size is 50 , which is larger than 30 .
(C) The sample size of 50 is less than $10 %$ of the residents in the city.
(D) The expected number of residents who regularly recycle is 16, and the expected number of residents who do not regularly recycle is 34 , and both numbers are at least 10 .
(E) The observed number of residents who regularly recycle is 28 , and the observed number of residents who do not regularly recycle is 22 , and both numbers are at least 10 .

A group of farmers wants to estimate the mean length of carrots grown on their farms. The farmers will select a random sample of carrots from the farms and will measure each carrot's length, in inches, and compute the mean and standard deviation of the sample.

Assuming the conditions for inference are met, which of the following is the most appropriate method to use for such an estimate?
(A) A one-sample $t$-interval for a population mean
(B) A one-sample $t$-interval for a sample mean
(C) A one-sample $z$-interval for a population mean
(D). A one-sample $z$-interval for a population proportion
(E) A one-sample $z$-interval for a sample proportion

Scores from a robotics competition have a mean of 19.9 points and a standard deviation of 7.2 points. Scores from an art competition have a mean of 20.2 points and a standard deviation of 5.7 points. Dominic enters the competitions and gets a score of 27 in robotics and a score of 26 in art.

Based on Dominic's standardized scores, in which competition did Dominic have a better performance?
(A) Robotics, because Dominic's standardized score in robotics is approximately 0.99 , while his standardized score in art is approximately 0.85 .
(B) Robotics, because Dominic's standardized score in robotics is approximately 1.19, while his standardized score in art is approximately 1.02.
(C) Art, because Dominic's standardized score in art is approximately 1.19, while his standardized score in robotics is approximately 0.85 .
(D) Art, because Dominic's standardized score in art is approximately 1.02, while his standardized score in robotics is approximately 0.99 .
(E) Art, because Dominic's standardized score in art is approximately 0.99, while his standardized score in robotics is approximately $1 . 0 2$.

A professional sports league has 30 teams. A fan of one of the teams is interested in the mean yearly salary of players on that team. The fan obtains the yearly salary of each player for all 28 players on the team.

Which of the following best describes the fan's sampling plan?
(A) Simple random sample
(B) Stratified random sample, with teams as strata
(C) Cluster sample, with teams as clusters
(D) Systematic random sample
(E) Census

In an experiment, Jaden, a statistics student, wants to investigate whether listening to music while playing a game of chess results in a game with more total moves. Jaden's large college has 200 students who play chess and are willing to participate in the experiment. He allows the players to decide whether they will play a chess game against a computer program while listening to music or will play a chess game against the same computer program while not listening to music. The total number of moves it takes for each chess game will be recorded.

Which of the following statements best describes why this is not a well-designed experiment?
(A) The subjects cannot be blind to the treatment because they will know whether they are listening to music.
(B) The treatments were not randomly assigned.
(C) There is not a control group of players who do not play chess but do listen to music.
(D) There was no replication because each player plays only one game against the computer program.
(E) The players were not randomly selected.

In a certain game, a player wins a prize by randomly picking a red marble from a bag of differently colored marbles. The probability that a player will win a prize on a given play of the game is 0.26 .

Assuming successive plays of the game are independent, which of the following statements is true?
(A) If a player plays this game a very large number of times, the player will win a prize about 26% of the time
(B) If a player plays the game 100 times, the player will win a prize exactly 26 times.
(C) If a player does not win a prize in 25 consecutive plays, the player is guaranteed to win a prize on the $26{ }^{ {th }}$ play.
(D) It is impossible for the player to win a prize on two consecutive plays of the game.
(E) The player is guaranteed to win exactly one prize in 26 consecutive plays of the game.

Blue light is the wavelength of light given off by electronic devices and energyefficient lightbulbs. Researchers are interested in investigating the effect of blue light on sleep. The researchers conduct a study using 30 volunteers. There are two light settings used in the study: one with a high amount of blue light and one with a low amount of blue light. Ench volunteer will spend the night in the researchers' sleep lab on two different nights. On one of the nights, each volunteer will be exposed to one of the two light settings for 50 minutes prior to their usual bedtime. On another night, each volunteer will be exposed to the other light setting for 50 minutes prior to their usual bedtime. The light setting that is experienced first is randomized for each volunteer, After each night in the sleep lab, the amount of melatonin, a hormone associated with the sleep-wake cycle, is measured for each volunteer. When measuring the results, the researchers know which light setting each volunteer was exposed to each night.

Which experimental design or method are the researchers using for the study?
(A) Double-blind experiment
(B) Randomized complete block design, blocked by usual bedtime
(C) Completely randomized design
(D) Matched pairs design
(E) This is an observational study, not an experiment.

A researcher in a certain country claims that the proportion of people in their twenties (people aged 20 to 29 ) who can lift more than 200 pounds is greater than the proportion of people in their forties (people aged 40 to 49) who can lift more than 200 pounds. In a random sample of people in their twenties living in that country, 31 percent could lift more than 200 pounds. In a separate random sample of people in their forties living in the country, 22 percent could lift more than 200 pounds.

Let $p_{1}$ be the proportion of all people in their twenties living in the country who can lift more than 200 pounds.

Let $p_{2}$ be the proportion of all people in their forties living in the country who can lift more than 200 pounds.

Which of the following are the appropriate null and alternative hypotheses for testing the researcher's claim about these two age groups?
(A) $H_{0}: p_{1}=0.31$
$H_{a}: p_{1}<0.31$
(B) $H_{0}: p_{1}=0.22$
$H_{a}: p_{2}>0.22$
(C) $H_{0}: p_{2}=0.22$
$H_{a}: p_{2}>0.22$
(D) $H_{0}: p_{1}=p_{2}$
$H_{a}: p_{1}p_{2}$

Many cities are hiring artists to create asphalt art, in which artists paint murals directly on certain roads in hopes of getting people to slow down and follow the speed limit along those roads. During a 24 -hour period, a researcher measured the speeds of all drivers who drove on randomly selected roads. Some roads had art, and some roads did not have art. Each road had a speed limit of 35 miles per hour (mph). The distributions of speed for both types of roads are displayed in the following boxplots.

Based on the boxplots, which of the following is a true statement?
(A) Because the speed of the first quartile on the roads with art is less than the minimum speed on the roads without art, it is not likely that drivers on roads with art travel at slower speeds.
(B) Because the range of the speeds for roads with art and the range of the speeds for roads without art are each approximately 20 mph , it is likely that drivers on roads with art do not travel at slower speeds.
(C) Because the interquartile range of the speeds on the roads with art is less than the interquartile range of the speeds on the roads without art, it is likely that drivers on roads with art travel at slower speeds.
(D) Because the maximum speed on the roads with art is greater than the median speed on the roads without art, it is likely that drivers on roads with art travel at slower speeds.
(E) Because each value of the five-number summary for the roads with art is less than the corresponding value of the five-number summary for the roads without art, it is likely that drivers on roads with art travel at slower speeds.

Information obtained from a random sample of 40 entry-level lawyers working in a certain country was used to calculate a 95 percent confidence interval for the true mean salary of all entry-level lawyers in the country. The confidence interval is $(\$ 56,100, \$ 58,900)$.

The owner of a large peach orchard has both genetically modified (GM) peach trees and traditional peach trees in the orchard. The orchard has hundreds of each type of peach tree. (E) A decision cannot be made because the data are based on a census. A random sample of Fridays would be required.
